findings.issue: shopifySteps declares a single op `productVariant` that `consumes: "variant external id"`, but for product-scoped subscriptions (`item_scope=product`) the widget passes a product external id — not a variant id — in `item_external_id`. `productVariant` requires a variant GID; it cannot accept a product GID. The widget state GET requestShape passes only `item_external_id` and `item_scope`, so there is no separate variant id available when scope is "product". The coding agent has no resolved op to check product-level availability, leaving the widget unable to suppress itself on in-stock product-scoped items.
findings.fix: Add a second shopifyStep using the `product` query (consuming `item_external_id` when `item_scope=product`) and note in the step sequence that the agent must branch: call `productVariant` when scope=variant and call `product` (checking whether any variant is available) when scope=product.

findings.issue: `keyedByColumns: ["id"]` places no structural constraint on `item_external_id` for pending rows. The trigger idempotency promises "if an unprocessed restock event already exists for the item, treat the event as a no-op," but that guarantee is only as strong as the application's check-then-insert logic. Concurrent webhook deliveries (Shopify routinely delivers duplicates within milliseconds) both pass the check before either commits, inserting two pending restock events for the same item. Both are then picked up by the schedule job and every waiting subscriber is notified twice — the exact double-blast the dedup design is meant to prevent.
findings.fix: Change `keyedByColumns` to `["item_external_id", "status"]` and add a column `status` purpose note clarifying that the uniqueness is intentionally conditional on the pending state; alternatively, add a dedicated `pending_restock_item_lock` table keyed by `["item_external_id"]` and cleared on processing, giving the DB a single-row race guard the application logic alone cannot provide.

findings.issue: `kind: "compute"` is declared for a capability whose description reads "Claim pending restock events and allocate notifications to the front of each item's signup-ordered queue … deferring the rest." Per the spec, `compute` is "pure logic over data already in hand"; this capability reads from the DB (`restock_events`, `waitlist_subscriptions`), writes claimed status transitions (usesWorkflow), triggers email sends to external subscribers, and inserts `notifications` rows. Tagging it as `compute` tells the coding agent it may skip write-path scaffolding (DB transactions, error rollback) and the workflow claim/complete/fail wiring that `usesWorkflow: true` demands.
findings.fix: Change `kind` to `"write"` to correctly signal that this capability mutates DB state and must be wrapped in the workflow claim/complete/fail lifecycle.

findings.issue: `usesWorkflow: true` is set, which binds the coding agent to the platform workflow helper (atomic claim/complete/fail/sweepStale). However, this capability only records a final terminal outcome (sent / bounced / failed) on a row that was already claimed by `process-restock-queue`. Invoking the workflow helper's claim step a second time on a row that is already mid-flight is a misuse of the helper's protocol and will conflict with the open claim held by `process-restock-queue`, potentially causing a double-claim error or a lost-update on the status field.
findings.fix: Set `usesWorkflow: false` on `record-notification-outcome` and describe it as a plain status-update write; keep `usesWorkflow: true` exclusively on `process-restock-queue`, which owns the full claim→send→complete/fail lifecycle for each notification row.
